blocks.x: Henry VIII Relied on This Courtier to Enforce His Orders During the English Reformation. Behind the Scenes, the Tudor Politician Defied His King by Secretly Saving a Catholic Text
A newly discovered fragment suggests that John Gage preserved a 15th-century religious manuscript, keeping it “safe when he was meant to destroy books precisely like this one”

Meilan Solly
| Senior Associate Digital Editor, History
September 21, 2026 3:08 p.m.

https://th-thumbnailer.cdn-si-edu.com/CZvm6hXvYP9wWJ-O18PyIIWfBfI=/1026x684/filters:focal(750x500:751x501)/https://tf-cmsv2-smithsonianmag-media.s3.amazonaws.com/filer_public/9a/87/9a87a020-0686-4a21-9b46-712a66884535/fix.png
blocks.c: Pages from a manuscript of Nicholas Love's Mirror of the Blessed Life of Jesus Christ

blocks.x: In August 1533, an English courtier named John Gage requested permission to leave Henry VIII’s court, finding himself “more disposed to serve God than the world,” in the words of a friend. A few months later, the Spanish ambassador reported that Gage had “retired to a Carthusian convent” with the intention of taking holy vows.

The exact circumstances of Gage’s departure from court remain unclear, but as historian David Potter wrote in a 2002 journal article, the timing of his absence might indicate that this “conventionally pious” courtier disapproved of the Tudor king’s decision to break with the Catholic Church and cast aside his first wife, Catherine of Aragon, in favor of Anne Boleyn. Regardless of Gage’s personal views, he soon abandoned his plans to become a friar, instead playing an active role in the dissolution of the monasteries, Henry’s campaign to seize the Church of England’s riches for himself.

How did Gage balance his apparent Catholic sympathies with his work on behalf of the reform-minded king? A new study published in the journal Notes and Queries suggests that the courtier coped by engaging in a covert act of disobedience: namely, preserving a Catholic text that he’d been sent to destroy.

https://th-thumbnailer.cdn-si-edu.com/GHXmsVR6wp0D6MGfwWFvI4V8KE4=/fit-in/1072x0/filters:focal(537x747:538x748)/https://tf-cmsv2-smithsonianmag-media.s3.amazonaws.com/filer_public/7c/c6/7cc64212-d780-42af-8a0c-3bedb1d3b9b2/sir_john_gage_english_courtier_and_politician_1479-1556.jpg
blocks.c: A Hans Holbein sketch of John Gage

blocks.x: “The dissolution of the monasteries led to the destruction of many books, but others were taken and then circulated through informal networks,” says first author Katie Walter, a literary scholar at the University of Sussex, in a statement. “By keeping this book on his shelf, John Gage and his family were part of a much bigger secret effort to preserve Catholic literature and knowledge.”

Walter and co-author James Wade, of the University of Cambridge, found the telltale pages hidden in plain sight at the Keep archive in Brighton. Although researchers have known for decades that a fragment from Nicholas Love’s Mirror of the Blessed Life of Jesus Christ was housed somewhere in Sussex, cataloging errors had prevented them from determining its exact location. The study’s authors not only found the six missing pages but also tracked down the medieval manuscript that originally contained the fragment.

“Once we realized what [the pages] were and the book that they came from … we started looking to extant manuscripts of the Mirror to match it up, and we found the match,” Wade tells Scientific American’s Adam Kovac.

https://th-thumbnailer.cdn-si-edu.com/ErcOdgaQzOQRXuoCeOkf-g3k6GM=/fit-in/1072x0/filters:focal(1077x718:1078x719)/https://tf-cmsv2-smithsonianmag-media.s3.amazonaws.com/filer_public/2c/05/2c05163d-9dc0-40ec-bebd-557e8dd79d5d/dr-katie-walter-and-dr-james-wade-with-the-fragment-in-the-kee-848f3e8f7880b7701898d4377d98e6d7.jpg
blocks.c: James Wade and Katie Walter with the manuscript fragment housed at the Keep archive in Brighton

blocks.x: Yale University’s Beinecke Library acquired the text from collector Toshiyuki Takamiya in 2017; Takamiya, for his part, had purchased it at auction in 1976. Exactly when the Keep fragment was separated from the rest of the manuscript is unknown, but Walter and Wade note that it must have taken place “between Gage’s acquisition and the manuscript’s rebinding in the 19th century.”
https://th-thumbnailer.cdn-si-edu.com/nRqTzr50w4nzzo3Dnmea7j0B9nE=/fit-in/200x200/filters:no_upscale()/https://tf-cmsv2-smithsonianmag-media.s3.amazonaws.com/accounts/headshot/meilan_headshot2.png

The most striking feature of the Yale manuscript appears on its final page, which likely lists the book’s owners. Gage’s signature appears alongside the names of two “religious women,” testifying to his acquisition of the Catholic text, according to the statement.

Love was a Yorkshire monk who translated a popular Franciscan Latin text into Middle English in the early 15th century. His Mirror was “endowed with a specially privileged status,” licensed by an archbishop “as an implied alternative to the Lollard Bible, the reading of which had been restricted,” literary scholar Kantik Ghosh wrote in a 2017 book chapter. (Lollardy was a proto-Protestant religious movement that espoused radical views for the era, including the belief that the Bible should be freely available in English rather than Latin.)

https://th-thumbnailer.cdn-si-edu.com/MWItkx_3vBXc8WMYQD6qlzcrIyU=/fit-in/1072x0/filters:focal(455x286:456x287)/https://tf-cmsv2-smithsonianmag-media.s3.amazonaws.com/filer_public/27/45/27456a77-88e0-4dc8-bea7-e82bf32b3bca/close-up-of-john-gage-signature-in-takamiya-ms20_beinecke-rare-a5b11be11a09a7507824125001ee0dfe.jpg
blocks.c: A close-up view of Gage's signature in the Yale manuscript

blocks.x: “It was a hugely popular work of English prose in the 15th century, and the reason it’s so important is because it’s right on the fulcrum of orthodox and heterodox belief,” Wade tells Scientific American. “It becomes a lightning rod for judging whether someone is a heretic or not.”

A century later, during the English Reformation, Love’s Mirror came under scrutiny by religious radicals who objected to its treatment of such issues as confession and the sacrament of communion. Despite this shift, at least medieval 65 copies of the text survive today—an impressive figure that shows “how a work that became suspicious and dangerous for some could also be valued and preserved by others,” Wade says in the statement.

Beyond his efforts on the crown’s behalf during the Reformation, Gage held multiple prominent positions in the kingdom, including comptroller of the royal household, constable of the Tower of London and member of the Privy Council.
Did you know? John Gage and Thomas Cromwell
Gage rose to prominence in part thanks to his relationship with Thomas Cromwell, Henry’s chief adviser and an architect of the English Reformation.
Gage carried out Cromwell’s orders despite their religious differences. After Cromwell’s execution in 1540, Gage received some of the fallen minister’s lands.

After Henry’s death in 1547, Gage served his heir, the young Protestant king Edward VI, on an on-and-off basis but was only fully restored to royal favor upon the accession of Edward’s Catholic sister, Mary I, in 1553. “There is every reason to suppose he welcomed the return of Catholicism, and almost immediately we see the fountain of royal patronage opened up again,” Potter wrote in his paper. Gage died in 1556 at age 76.

“Gage had a very long career in a highly turbulent court,” Wade says in the statement. “He survived when many other very shrewd people did not. And he made a fortune in the process. But he’s also this incredibly conflicted man, because he remained a Catholic throughout the Reformation. He’s got all this power and bureaucratic savvy combined with a risky conviction in his faith. Somehow he manages to reconcile these two things and survive.”
